exam: A patient from a rural Ugandan village presents with fever, vomiting, and a rash. What is your immediate management step — isolate the patient, start broad‑spectrum antibiotics, and arrange PCR testing.
How does Ebola virus cause coagulopathy — endothelial damage leading to tissue factor release and consumption of clotting factors; differentiate from DIC of severe malaria.
What laboratory result would most strongly support Ebola over severe malaria — positive RT‑PCR for Ebola RNA; malaria smear may be negative or low parasitaemia.
Why is aggressive fluid replacement critical in early EVD — prevents hypovolemic shock from profuse vomiting/diarrhea; avoid over‑resuscitation that can worsen edema.
A colleague suggests giving high‑dose vitamin K to stop bleeding. Explain why this is ineffective — bleeding is due to consumptive coagulopathy, not vitamin K deficiency.
During an outbreak, a health worker refuses PPE citing shortage. What should you do — enforce infection‑control policy, provide PPE, and report breach to infection‑control team.

Explain how you would differentiate Ebola from Lassa fever clinically — Lassa often has milder bleeding, more prominent pharyngitis, and a different geographic pattern; both require PCR for definitive diagnosis.
What are the key components of safe burial in an Ebola outbreak — use PPE, disinfect body, avoid direct contact, and involve trained burial teams.
ai.title: Ebola Virus Disease
ai.subject: Microbiology & immunology
ai.summary: Ebola virus causes a severe hemorrhagic fever with high mortality. Transmission is through direct contact with infected body fluids. Diagnosis relies on PCR or antigen detection, and supportive care is the mainstay of treatment.

b: High case‑fatality rates (30‑90%) depending on strain and care
sections.p: Ebola virus disease (EVD) is a rare but deadly viral hemorrhagic fever endemic to Central and West Africa. Outbreaks occur in low‑resource settings where infection control is limited.

b: Four species cause human disease: Zaire, Sudan, Bundibugyo, Tai Forest
Reservoir: fruit bats; primates act as amplifying hosts
sections.p: Ebola virus is a filamentous, enveloped, negative‑sense RNA virus of the Filoviridae family. It is highly unstable outside the host but survives in blood and bodily fluids for days.

b: Sexual transmission can persist for months in survivors
sections.p: Transmission occurs by direct contact with blood, secretions, organs, or contaminated surfaces. The virus enters via mucous membranes or breaks in the skin, replicates in macrophages, then spreads systemically.

b: Diagnostic criteria: fever + ≥2 of headache, vomiting, diarrhea, rash, or bleeding + epidemiologic link
Severity staged by WHO: mild (no bleeding), moderate (bleeding, hypotension), severe (organ failure, shock)
Common differentials in East Africa: severe malaria, typhoid fever, Lassa fever, bacterial sepsis, dengue
sections.p: EVD presents with a prodrome of fever, fatigue, myalgia, followed by gastrointestinal loss, rash, and coagulopathy. Severe disease features shock, multi‑organ failure, and hemorrhage.
Laboratory confirmation is essential but often delayed in low‑resource settings. Clinical suspicion guides isolation and supportive care while awaiting results.

t.b: Confirms active infection; a positive result confirms EVD, a negative early result does not rule out disease

t.a: If PCR unavailable, send dried blood spots to reference lab
t.b: Allows delayed confirmation; meanwhile manage as probable EVD

b: Fluid resuscitation with balanced crystalloids; avoid excessive colloids
Broad‑spectrum antibiotics only if bacterial co‑infection suspected
Experimental antivirals (e.g., remdesivir) may be used in trial settings; not standard care
Viral‑specific monoclonal antibodies (e.g., ansuvimab) when accessible
sections.p: No licensed antiviral is widely available; care focuses on aggressive supportive therapy and infection control.

t.b: Breaks transmission chains in the community

Remember that a normal PT/INR early does not exclude later coagulopathy
